case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a bankruptcy debtor’s failure to disclose a pending civil claim can be treated as non-inadvertent (and thus judicially estopped) based only on the debtor’s knowledge of the claim and a motive to conceal, or whether courts must instead make a holistic, circumstance-specific assessment consistent with New Hampshire v. Maine.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal common-law doctrine of judicial estoppel as applied in the bankruptcy context (implicating Bankruptcy Code disclosure/estate-administration duties, e.g., 11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541, and related rules requiring accurate schedules).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Keathley argues that the Fifth Circuit applied an overbroad, near-automatic judicial-estoppel rule that treats nondisclosure as intentional whenever the debtor knew of the facts and had a motive to conceal (a motive nearly always present in bankruptcy), which conflicts with New Hampshire v. Maine’s equitable, discretionary, multi-factor approach and improperly bars personal-injury claims without considering the full context (including later disclosure and the interests of creditors and the bankruptcy estate). He and supporting amici emphasize that rigid estoppel punishes creditors and can thwart proper administration of estate assets, and that any remedy for nondisclosure should be handled through bankruptcy mechanisms (reopening the case, trustee control of the claim, sanctions) rather than forfeiting the cause of action outright.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Buddy Ayers Construction argues that judicial estoppel properly bars Keathley’s suit because the record shows deliberate, repeated nondisclosure of separately pending personal-injury and workers’ compensation claims in bankruptcy schedules, with disclosure occurring only after the defendant sought summary judgment—facts that, in respondent’s view, demonstrate bad faith and satisfy New Hampshire v. Maine’s core concern with protecting judicial integrity. Respondent also frames the question more broadly as whether judicial estoppel may apply regardless of direct evidence of subjective bad faith, contending that allowing such claims to proceed after concealment would incentivize manipulation of the bankruptcy system and undermine honest disclosure obligations.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s deterrence and integrity-of-the-process argument has real force: bankruptcy depends on truthful schedules, and a regime that permits “amend when caught” can invite manipulation. But New Hampshire v. Maine, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, frames judicial estoppel as a flexible, equitable doctrine with nonexclusive factors; the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-generic-motive approach risks hardening that flexibility into a near-irrebuttable presumption because “motive” is endemic in bankruptcy. A narrower rule—treating nondisclosure, timing of correction, and repetition as highly probative of bad faith while still requiring a holistic record-based inquiry including whether the bankruptcy court adopted the earlier position—preserves institutional legitimacy and avoids forfeitures that harm creditors, as Justice Sotomayor underscores. Alito’s concern can be addressed within that framework because courts remain free to estop where the full record shows calculated concealment, without converting a common bankruptcy incentive into a dispositive legal rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s integrity-of-the-process argument is weighty, but it does not justify the Fifth Circuit’s near-automatic “knowledge + motive” inference, because in bankruptcy “motive” is effectively ubiquitous and thus cannot do the individualized work New Hampshire v. Maine demands. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, New Hampshire rejects inflexible prerequisites and requires a circumstance-specific inquiry, including whether the bankruptcy court actually adopted the earlier position and whether the omission was truly inadvertent on the full record. Textually, the Bankruptcy Code (including §§ 521 and 541) already sets out disclosure duties, estate ownership, and remedial mechanisms; layering a forfeiture-like federal common-law presumption risks reallocating estate assets away from creditors and toward alleged tortfeasors. Estoppel should remain available where the record shows deliberate manipulation, but not as a quasi-per se rule triggered by generalized motive.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that New Hampshire v. Maine rejects “inflexible prerequisites” and speaks in nonexclusive factors, but that cuts against adopting any rigid intent-element requirement as well; it leaves room for strong inferences from circumstantial evidence where the integrity of the bankruptcy system is at stake. Their concern that “motive” is ubiquitous in bankruptcy is forceful, yet the Fifth Circuit’s inference is not motive-alone—it is motive plus knowledge of the claim plus a telling sequence of omission and only belated correction after being challenged, which in my view reasonably supports a finding of non-inadvertence without direct proof of subjective bad faith. Justice Sotomayor’s creditor-windfall argument underscores a real consequence, but the answer is not to weaken estoppel across the board; bankruptcy tools (trustee substitution/reopening) can address creditor harm in appropriate cases while preserving estoppel as a meaningful deterrent against “amend when caught.” Given New Hampshire’s core purpose—protecting judicial integrity—I do not think it forbids a circuit from treating this combination of facts as highly, even presumptively, indicative of strategic nondisclosure.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that bankruptcy depends on candid disclosure and that “amend when caught” behavior can threaten the integrity of the process, but his proposed reliance on a strong knowledge-plus-motive inference effectively hardens a flexible equitable doctrine into a near-forfeiture rule in a setting where motive is virtually universal. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, New Hampshire v. Maine rejects “inflexible prerequisites” and instead demands a circumstance-specific inquiry—including whether the bankruptcy court actually adopted the earlier position and whether the omission reflects mistake versus manipulation—so the Fifth Circuit’s quasi-per se presumption is a poor fit with our precedent. Pragmatically, automatic estoppel predictably harms creditors and vulnerable debtors by extinguishing estate value and handing windfalls to alleged wrongdoers, while bankruptcy’s own tools (reopening, trustee control, sanctions) can protect the system without categorical forfeiture. I therefore remain with Petitioner: nondisclosure is powerful evidence of bad faith, but it should not be dispositive as a matter of law absent a holistic record showing deliberate concealment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that bankruptcy’s disclosure regime makes omissions uniquely corrosive and that circumstantial evidence (knowledge, incentive, late correction) can strongly suggest strategic behavior; that point must carry real weight in the estoppel analysis. But as the Chief Justice notes, New Hampshire v. Maine rejects “inflexible prerequisites,” and a knowledge-plus-generic-motive rule in bankruptcy risks becoming functionally dispositive because motive is nearly always present—collapsing the mistake/inadvertence inquiry the precedent preserves. Justice Sotomayor’s practical concern reinforces the doctrinal one: a near-automatic estoppel can wipe out estate value and hand defendants a windfall even though the Code’s own tools (reopening, trustee control, sanctions) can deter and remedy concealment without categorical forfeiture. The more coherent, workable middle ground is to treat nondisclosure and belated amendment as highly probative of bad faith while requiring a holistic, record-based intent assessment before estopping the claim.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that bankruptcy nondisclosure can threaten the integrity of the judicial process and that circumstantial evidence may suffice to show manipulation; equity need not demand a confession of bad faith. But his proposed reliance on “knowledge + motive” risks functionally hardening a ubiquitous bankruptcy incentive into an almost conclusive presumption, contrary to New Hampshire v. Maine’s insistence (as the Chief notes) that judicial estoppel resists “inflexible prerequisites” and requires a genuinely record-based, circumstance-specific assessment, including whether the bankruptcy court adopted the earlier position. As Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Bankruptcy Code already supplies targeted remedies (trustee control, reopening, sanctions) that protect creditors and the system without courts effectively extinguishing estate assets via a broad federal common-law forfeiture rule. I would therefore reject the Fifth Circuit’s quasi-per se inference while leaving ample room to estop where the full record demonstrates deliberate concealment and judicial acceptance of the prior position.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s deterrence and integrity-of-the-process point has real force in bankruptcy, where accurate schedules are indispensable and “amend when caught” behavior is troubling. But as the Chief Justice Roberts stresses, New Hampshire v. Maine makes judicial estoppel a discretionary, equitable doctrine that resists inflexible prerequisites; the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-generic-motive inference risks hardening equity into a near-irrebuttable presumption because “motive” is virtually always present in bankruptcy. That categorical approach also threatens the Code’s creditor-protective structure by effectively wiping out an estate asset and gifting a windfall to civil defendants when reopening, trustee control, and sanctions can address nondisclosure without automatic forfeiture. I would keep estoppel available for deliberate concealment—timing, repetition, and post-challenge amendments can be powerful evidence—but require the holistic, record-based intent inquiry Roberts and Barrett describe rather than treating knowledge + generic motive as dispositive.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that bankruptcy nondisclosure uniquely threatens the integrity of judicial proceedings and that circumstantial evidence can support estoppel without direct proof of subjective bad faith. But New Hampshire v. Maine—invoked by the Chief Justice—treats judicial estoppel as an equitable, discretionary doctrine with nonexclusive factors, and the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-generic-motive approach effectively hardens that discretion into a near-automatic presumption because “motive” is endemic in bankruptcy. As Justice Thomas notes, the Bankruptcy Code already supplies targeted mechanisms (estate ownership, reopening, trustee control, sanctions) that protect the process and creditors; converting estoppel into a forfeiture-like rule risks reallocating estate value away from creditors and toward alleged wrongdoers without the circumstance-specific inquiry New Hampshire demands. The better rule is to treat nondisclosure and belated correction as powerful evidence of bad faith, but not dispositive as a matter of law absent a holistic record showing deliberate manipulation and meaningful judicial acceptance of the earlier position.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that bankruptcy depends on truthful disclosure and that courts must deter “wait-and-see” concealment to protect the integrity of the process. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, New Hampshire v. Maine treats judicial estoppel as a flexible, equitable doctrine that resists inflexible prerequisites; the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-generic-motive inference risks becoming effectively irrebuttable because “motive” is endemic in bankruptcy, collapsing the mistake/inadvertence inquiry. From my pragmatic, fairness-centered perspective, that near-categorical approach also produces perverse consequences—extinguishing estate value and harming creditors—when bankruptcy tools (reopening, trustee/trustee substitution, sanctions) can both protect the system and preserve claims while still permitting estoppel on a developed record showing actual manipulation. I therefore continue to favor a holistic, intent-focused assessment where timing, repetition, and belated amendment are highly probative but not dispositive as a matter of law.

John Roberts.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable, discretionary doctrine that turns on a case-specific assessment, warning against applying it through "inflexible prerequisites" and emphasizing context, including whether the prior position was adopted by a court and whether any inconsistency was the product of mistake or inadvertence. A near-automatic rule inferring non-inadvertence from knowledge plus a generic bankruptcy motive risks departing from that framework and unnecessarily forfeiting claims in a way that can harm creditors and disrupt estate administration under the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure and estate provisions, including 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541. A narrower disposition is to require a holistic intent-focused inquiry—leaving room for estoppel in cases of deliberate concealment—while permitting bankruptcy tools (reopening, trustee control, sanctions) to address nondisclosure without reflexively barring the claim. That approach better preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to this Court’s equitable precedent and avoiding a categorical presumption not grounded in New Hampshire.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is a federal common-law, equitable doctrine, and this Court in New Hampshire v. Maine emphasized that it is not reducible to a mechanical rule but instead turns on circumstance-specific considerations, including whether the party’s later position reflects an attempt to mislead the courts. The Fifth Circuit’s near-automatic inference of non-inadvertence from mere knowledge of a claim plus a generic “motive to conceal” (a motive that will exist in nearly every bankruptcy) departs from that discretionary framework and risks converting equity into an irrebuttable presumption. Whatever the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure duties under 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541, the proper response to a deficient schedule is ordinarily to vindicate the estate’s interests through bankruptcy administration (e.g., amendment, reopening, trustee control), not to impose a categorical forfeiture untethered from the debtor’s actual intent. Because New Hampshire requires a holistic inquiry rather than a per se rule, I would reverse.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, common-law doctrine designed to protect the integrity of the judicial process, and New Hampshire v. Maine emphasizes flexible, circumstance-specific factors rather than a rigid, intent-element requirement. In the bankruptcy setting, the debtor’s statutory duties of full and accurate disclosure (11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541) make omissions of known claims especially serious; when the debtor knew of the claim, had an obvious incentive to keep it out of the estate, and disclosed only after an adversary raised the omission, it is reasonable to treat the nondisclosure as non-inadvertent on the record as a whole. Requiring direct proof of subjective bad faith would unduly hamstring courts’ ability to deter manipulation of bankruptcy proceedings and would create perverse incentives for debtors to “wait and see” until caught. The Fifth Circuit’s approach, applied to repeated nondisclosure and belated correction, falls within New Hampshire’s discretionary framework and appropriately vindicates the disclosure regime’s practical consequences for honest estate administration.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, discretionary doctrine aimed at preventing deliberate manipulation of the courts, not a near-automatic forfeiture rule, and New Hampshire v. Maine requires a circumstance-specific assessment rather than a presumption of bad faith from mere knowledge plus an always-present bankruptcy “motive.” In the bankruptcy context, converting nondisclosure into automatic estoppel can unfairly deprive debtors of meritorious claims and, critically, reduce recoveries for creditors—the very parties the disclosure duties in 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541 are designed to protect—while handing an unjust windfall to alleged tortfeasors. Bankruptcy courts have targeted tools (reopening, trustee administration of the claim, sanctions) that can remedy nondisclosure without extinguishing the estate asset, and the Fifth Circuit’s rigid approach undermines those practical, remedial mechanisms. The proper course is to vacate and remand for a holistic inquiry into intent and surrounding circumstances consistent with New Hampshire v. Maine.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine characterizes judicial estoppel as an equitable, discretionary doctrine guided by nonexclusive factors, and it cautions against rigid application divorced from context—especially where the issue is whether a prior position was taken through “inadvertence or mistake.” In the bankruptcy setting, a near-automatic “knowledge + motive” inference effectively collapses that inquiry because a motive to conceal is almost always present given the disclosure duties in 11 U.S.C. §§ 521(a)(1) and 541, turning an equitable doctrine into a rule-like forfeiture. A holistic assessment better fits New Hampshire’s framework and is more workable with the Bankruptcy Code’s own remedial tools (e.g., reopening and trustee control) that protect creditors rather than punishing them by wiping out estate value. Courts may still find bad faith and apply estoppel on an appropriate record, but they must do so through a circumstance-specific analysis rather than an irrebuttable or near-irrebuttable presumption.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, judge-made doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine instructs courts to apply it through a circumstance-specific inquiry rather than a near-automatic rule. The Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive presumption effectively converts a discretionary doctrine into something like a categorical forfeiture rule in bankruptcy—where “motive” will almost always exist—risking overreach inconsistent with the limited, case-by-case nature of federal common-law equity and with separation-of-powers principles. The Bankruptcy Code already supplies targeted tools for nondisclosure and estate administration, including disclosure duties under 11 U.S.C. § 521 and the estate’s ownership of claims under § 541, allowing reopening, trustee control, and sanctions without broadly extinguishing claims that may benefit creditors. Courts may still estop in appropriate cases, but they must assess the full record—including subsequent corrections and whether the bankruptcy court actually accepted the earlier position—consistent with New Hampshire v. Maine.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable, discretionary doctrine guided by multiple factors, not a near-automatic rule triggered whenever a bankruptcy debtor knew of a claim and had a generic motive to conceal. A knowledge-plus-motive presumption is especially problematic in bankruptcy, where some motive is almost always present, and it risks barring potentially valuable estate assets contrary to the Bankruptcy Code’s administration framework (including the debtor’s disclosure duties under 11 U.S.C. § 521 and the estate’s ownership of claims under 11 U.S.C. § 541). Consistent with history and tradition of equitable estoppel, courts should make a circumstance-specific assessment—considering, among other things, whether the bankruptcy court accepted the earlier position and whether later correction/reopening can protect creditors—rather than treating nondisclosure as per se non-inadvertent. That approach better preserves workability and the Court’s legitimacy by adhering to this Court’s precedent while leaving primary policing of disclosure failures to bankruptcy mechanisms.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, discretionary federal common-law doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine instructs courts to apply a circumstance-specific, multi-factor inquiry rather than a near-automatic rule. The Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive test effectively makes nondisclosure “non-inadvertent” in almost every bankruptcy case—because a debtor will virtually always have a theoretical motive to conceal—thereby collapsing the intent inquiry and displacing the holistic assessment New Hampshire requires. Although the Bankruptcy Code imposes serious disclosure duties (e.g., 11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541), the proper response to nondisclosure should account for context (including amendment, trustee administration, and creditor interests) rather than imposing an irrebuttable presumption that bars the cause of action. A rule faithful to New Hampshire preserves methodological consistency by treating intent and equity as fact-bound, not presumed from generalized incentives.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, discretionary doctrine that New Hampshire v. Maine instructs courts to apply through a circumstance-specific, multi-factor inquiry aimed at preventing intentional manipulation, not by imposing an effectively irrebuttable presumption of bad faith. Treating nondisclosure as “non-inadvertent” based solely on the debtor’s knowledge of the claim and a generic bankruptcy motive to conceal collapses the required distinction between intentional deceit and mistake, and risks procedurally unfair forfeiture without a meaningful opportunity to contest intent. A holistic approach better accounts for bankruptcy’s remedial tools and estate-administration interests under 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541 (including reopening, trustee control of the claim, and sanctions) rather than automatically extinguishing potentially valuable assets to the detriment of creditors. The Fifth Circuit’s near-automatic rule therefore conflicts with New Hampshire’s equitable framework and should be rejected in favor of a context-sensitive inquiry into bad faith and practical consequences.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court may apply judicial estoppel to bar a debtor’s later civil suit based on the debtor’s failure to disclose that claim in bankruptcy by presuming bad faith from knowledge and motive alone, or instead must conduct a holistic, circumstance-specific inquiry consistent with New Hampshire v. Maine.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal common-law doctrine of judicial estoppel (equitable doctrine), as applied in the bankruptcy disclosure context under the Bankruptcy Code’s debtor disclosure regime (e.g., 11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541) and related bankruptcy rules requiring complete schedules; supervisory role of U.S. Trustees under 28 U.S.C. § 586 is also implicated (as described by the United States).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Keathley argues that the Fifth Circuit applied an overly rigid judicial-estoppel rule that effectively presumes nondisclosure was intentional (and thus estoppel-worthy) whenever the debtor knew about the underlying facts and had a motive to conceal—without a full, holistic assessment of the record. He contends that New Hampshire v. Maine requires a flexible, equitable inquiry into all relevant circumstances (including context, explanations, bankruptcy case posture, corrective disclosures, and who would be harmed), and that automatic estoppel improperly punishes creditors and the bankruptcy estate by extinguishing potentially valuable assets rather than addressing nondisclosure through bankruptcy remedies or trustee administration.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Buddy Ayers Construction argues that judicial estoppel properly bars Keathley’s personal-injury suit because the evidence showed deliberate, repeated nondisclosure of known, separately pending personal-injury and workers’ compensation claims, with disclosure coming only after the defendant moved for summary judgment based on the omission. Respondent contends that courts may invoke judicial estoppel regardless of direct proof of subjective bad faith, because the bankruptcy nondisclosure itself—paired with knowledge and a clear incentive to hide assets—undermines judicial integrity; allowing the suit to proceed would reward concealment and encourage debtors to treat disclosure obligations as optional unless caught.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that bankruptcy’s disclosure regime depends on deterrence and that objective facts—especially correction only after an opponent raises nondisclosure—can strongly support an inference of manipulation. But Justice Thomas’s approach risks hardening that inference into a near-conclusive rule whenever a debtor has knowledge and some generic “motive,” which would be difficult to reconcile with New Hampshire v. Maine’s insistence that judicial estoppel is equitable and “not reducible to any general formulation.” Under a minimalist, precedent-centered approach, I would hold narrowly that knowledge and motive are probative but not dispositive, requiring courts to consider the full record (timing, bankruptcy posture, corrective steps, and creditor impact) before imposing the severe sanction of claim forfeiture that can extinguish estate value under § 541. The Code’s tailored tools (reopening, amendment, trustee control, sanctions) remain relevant circumstances in that equitable calculus, mitigating the need for an administrable but overly rigid estoppel shortcut.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point, pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch, is that New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as flexible and cautions against “inflexible prerequisites.” But that flexibility does not forbid courts from drawing strong, rebuttable inferences of bad faith from objective facts; in bankruptcy, the statutory scheme (11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541) makes nondisclosure of a known claim a serious, outcome-affecting inconsistency, and equity has long relied on such objective indicia to protect the integrity of judicial proceedings. Justice Sotomayor’s creditor-harm concern is real, yet it goes to tailoring the remedy (e.g., allowing trustee substitution or limiting estoppel’s reach) rather than to disabling estoppel where the debtor maintained nondisclosure until challenged. Under an originalist/textualist approach, nothing in the Code or New Hampshire compels a debtor-friendly “totality” requirement that would, in practice, make disclosure duties optional whenever motive can be characterized as ubiquitous.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest point from the other side, pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan, is that New Hampshire v. Maine warns against rigid “inflexible prerequisites” and that barring suit can harm creditors when the claim is estate property under § 541. But I do not read the Fifth Circuit’s approach as an irrebuttable presumption; it is a permissible inference from objective, legally significant facts—statutory disclosure duties under § 521, omission of a known claim through discharge, and “correction” only after an adversary raises estoppel—facts that strongly indicate manipulation without requiring courts to conduct a subjective-intent mini-trial in every case. Justice Sotomayor’s creditor-harm concern is real, yet as Justice Thomas notes it goes chiefly to remedy and case management (e.g., trustee substitution), not to whether a court may infer bad faith to protect judicial integrity; a rule that routinely excuses late disclosure risks inviting strategic nondisclosure and increasing costs that ultimately reduce creditor recoveries. New Hampshire’s flexibility allows courts to weigh circumstances, but it does not forbid reliance on commonsense inferences in a context where Congress has made disclosure mandatory and the inconsistency threatens the integrity of both the bankruptcy and judicial processes.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that bankruptcy’s disclosure regime depends on enforceable consequences and that sustained nondisclosure corrected only after a dispositive motion is powerful circumstantial evidence of manipulation. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, New Hampshire v. Maine warns that judicial estoppel’s equitable guideposts are not to harden into an almost-conclusive rule; in bankruptcy, “knowledge plus motive” risks becoming categorical because virtually every debtor has both, turning an inference into forfeiture. Justice Thomas’s point that the Code does not disable estoppel is correct, yet it does not answer the remedial mismatch I’m concerned about: rigid estoppel can extinguish estate value under § 541 and punish creditors rather than the wrongdoer when bankruptcy tools (trustee substitution, reopening, sanctions) can protect integrity without wiping out recoveries. I would therefore reverse a framework that treats knowledge-and-motive as effectively dispositive, while preserving courts’ ability to infer bad faith from the total record, including timing, explanations, and bankruptcy posture.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s deterrence/administrability point is the best case for Respondent, and I agree that in bankruptcy a debtor’s knowledge plus delayed correction can be powerful circumstantial evidence of manipulation. But Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor are right that New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as equitable and “not reducible to any general formulation,” so a knowledge-and-motive framework that operates in practice as near-dispositive is hard to reconcile with that precedent and with the Code’s structure making claims estate property under § 541 and imposing disclosure duties under § 521. Justice Thomas is also right that nothing in the Code disables estoppel, yet that cuts toward a tailored equitable application (including trustee substitution, reopening, and sanctions) rather than a rule that routinely extinguishes estate value and harms creditors who were not the wrongdoers. I would reverse and remand for a totality-of-circumstances inquiry where knowledge and motive are relevant but not outcome-determinative, preserving room to estop when the record shows intentional manipulation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s deterrence-and-administrability argument is the strongest for Respondent, and I agree that intent may be inferred from objective circumstances in bankruptcy where §§ 521 and 541 impose clear duties. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine “not reducible to any general formulation,” and the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive framework risks hardening that flexible inquiry into a near-automatic forfeiture whenever a debtor had any incentive to conceal—an incentive that is commonplace and thus insufficiently discriminating. Justice Thomas is right that nothing in the Code disables estoppel, yet the Code’s allocation of undisclosed claims to the estate counsels against an inflexible rule that can erase value belonging to creditors without a record-based finding of intentional manipulation; equity’s severe sanction should remain tied to the totality (timing, amendments, explanations, bankruptcy posture), not a proxy that functions like an irrebuttable presumption. I would reverse and remand for a circumstance-specific inquiry that permits strong inferences where warranted but preserves discretion consistent with New Hampshire.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Thomas rightly stress deterrence and the statutory disclosure duties in §§ 521 and 541; a debtor’s sustained nondisclosure of a known claim is powerful circumstantial evidence, and equity may draw commonsense inferences to protect judicial integrity. But Chief Justice Roberts’s point about New Hampshire v. Maine remains decisive for me: judicial estoppel is an equitable, flexible doctrine whose guideposts are “not reducible to any general formulation,” and the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive framework risks hardening into an almost-automatic forfeiture. That rigidity is especially troubling where the claim is estate property and estoppel can punish creditors more than the debtor, even though the Bankruptcy Code supplies narrower tools (reopening, trustee substitution/control, sanctions) to remedy nondisclosure without extinguishing value. I would reverse and remand for a totality-of-circumstances inquiry that preserves strong inferences of bad faith while keeping them rebuttable and context-sensitive.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s deterrence and administrability point is the strongest for Respondent: persistent nondisclosure of a known claim until confronted is powerful circumstantial evidence of manipulation, and courts need not conduct a subjective-intent mini-trial in every case. But Justice Roberts correctly anchors the doctrine in New Hampshire v. Maine’s insistence that judicial estoppel is an equitable, flexible remedy “not reducible to any general formulation,” which makes the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-generic-motive approach functionally too close to a near-automatic rule in a context where virtually every debtor has some motive. Justice Thomas is right that §§ 521 and 541 heighten the significance of nondisclosure and permit commonsense inferences, yet that statutory backdrop also underscores why a categorical estoppel forfeiture can misallocate estate value away from creditors and displace the Code’s tailored mechanisms (reopening, amendment, trustee administration, sanctions) absent a record-based, totality finding of intentional abuse. I would reverse only to the extent the lower court treated knowledge and motive as dispositive, while preserving broad discretion to infer bad faith from the full circumstances, including late correction after a dispositive motion.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability and deterrence argument is the strongest for Respondent: in bankruptcy, continued nondisclosure of a known claim until an opponent objects is often highly probative of manipulation. But under New Hampshire v. Maine, that probative inference cannot be allowed to harden into a quasi-presumption that displaces equity’s obligation to consider the full record—especially where, as Justice Sotomayor emphasizes, a forfeiture remedy can primarily punish creditors by extinguishing estate value that § 541 assigns to them, notwithstanding the Code’s disclosure duty in § 521. Justice Thomas is right that nothing in the Code disables judicial estoppel and that objective indicia matter; still, equity’s procedural fairness requires courts to test “knowledge and motive” against timing of correction, reliance on counsel, bankruptcy court posture, and alternative Code remedies (reopening, trustee administration, sanctions) before imposing the unusually severe consequence of claim forfeiture. On that pragmatic, consequences-sensitive view, the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-and-motive framework remains too rigid and warrants reversal and remand for a totality-based inquiry.

John Roberts.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as a flexible, equitable doctrine whose application turns on a circumstance-specific assessment, not a rigid presumption. In the bankruptcy-disclosure setting, a rule that effectively infers bad faith from “knowledge and motive” alone risks converting an equitable safeguard into a near-automatic forfeiture that may harm the estate and creditors—concerns the Code addresses through its own mechanisms requiring complete schedules and administration of estate property, see 11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541. To protect institutional legitimacy and preserve the narrow role of judicial estoppel, I would require courts to consider the totality of the circumstances (including corrective disclosures and the bankruptcy case posture) before barring the later suit.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is a federal common-law, equitable doctrine aimed at protecting the integrity of judicial proceedings by preventing a litigant from asserting inconsistent positions, and New Hampshire v. Maine recognizes that while the inquiry is equitable, courts may consider whether the later position is “clearly inconsistent” and whether acceptance of the earlier position would create a perception that a court was misled. In bankruptcy, Congress’s disclosure regime (11 U.S.C. §§ 521, 541) makes contingent and unliquidated claims property of the estate that must be scheduled; a debtor who proceeds as if no such asset exists, despite knowledge and the obvious incentive to conceal, takes a position incompatible with later pursuing that claim for personal benefit. Nothing in the Constitution’s text or the Bankruptcy Code compels courts to adopt a debtor-friendly presumption of “inadvertence” or to disable courts from drawing commonsense inferences from objective facts when policing abuse of the judicial process. Accordingly, the Fifth Circuit’s willingness to infer bad faith from knowledge and motive in this context is consistent with judicial estoppel’s purpose and with New Hampshire’s emphasis on preventing misuse of the courts.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, federal common-law doctrine aimed at protecting the integrity of the judicial process, and New Hampshire v. Maine permits courts to apply flexible guideposts without demanding direct proof of subjective intent. In the bankruptcy context, the debtor’s statutory duty to disclose all assets, including contingent and unliquidated claims, is central to the system’s operation under 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541, and a debtor’s knowledge of a claim coupled with the obvious incentive to conceal it provides a sufficiently reliable basis to infer bad faith where nondisclosure persists until an opposing party raises it. A rigid insistence on a full-blown, circumstance-by-circumstance inquiry in every case risks incentivizing strategic nondisclosure and imposes substantial practical costs on creditors, trustees, and courts, while undermining compliance with the disclosure regime. Given the repeated nondisclosure described here and the corrective disclosure only after a dispositive motion, applying judicial estoppel is an appropriate and practical means of deterring abuse and preserving judicial integrity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, discretionary doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine requires a flexible, circumstance-specific inquiry rather than a near-conclusive presumption of bad faith from knowledge plus motive alone. In the bankruptcy context, rigid estoppel rules can unfairly extinguish assets of the estate and harm creditors—vulnerable parties in this system—when the Bankruptcy Code already supplies targeted remedies and administrative oversight to address nondisclosure (including the debtor’s disclosure duties under 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541 and trustee/U.S. Trustee supervision under 28 U.S.C. § 586). Courts should examine the full record—timing, explanations, corrective amendments, and who bears the costs—before imposing the harsh sanction of barring a potentially meritorious civil claim. Presuming intent categorically risks turning an equitable doctrine into a punitive forfeiture, undermining fairness and access to justice in a way New Hampshire rejects.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, federal common-law doctrine that New Hampshire v. Maine instructs courts to apply flexibly based on “all the circumstances,” not through a near-automatic rule that treats knowledge plus a generic bankruptcy “motive” as dispositive proof of bad faith. In the bankruptcy context, the debtor’s disclosure duties under 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541 are real and enforceable, but the appropriate response to nondisclosure must remain workable and coherent with bankruptcy administration—often through trustee control, amendment, or other bankruptcy remedies—rather than an irrebuttable presumption that extinguishes potentially estate-owned claims to the detriment of creditors. A court may infer intent from the record, but it must do so holistically (including timing of correction, explanations, bankruptcy posture, and who would be harmed), consistent with New Hampshire’s circumstance-specific approach. The Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-and-motive-only framework is too rigid to satisfy that equitable standard and risks turning judicial estoppel from a narrow integrity-protecting tool into a punitive forfeiture regime.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is a federal common-law equitable doctrine that this Court in New Hampshire v. Maine described as discretionary and circumstance-specific, with factors that are "not reducible to any general formulation" and aimed at preventing intentional manipulation of the judicial process rather than punishing mistake. A rule that presumes bad faith from knowledge and motive alone in the bankruptcy context effectively converts that flexible doctrine into a near-mechanical forfeiture, contrary to equity’s traditional aversion to rigid rules and inconsistent with New Hampshire’s holistic approach. The Bankruptcy Code already supplies targeted tools to address nondisclosure and protect creditors—e.g., the estate’s ownership of undisclosed claims under 11 U.S.C. § 541 and the debtor’s disclosure duties under § 521—making it especially important that courts not use an inflexible estoppel presumption to extinguish value that may belong to the estate. Consistent with separation-of-powers concerns and the limited role of federal common law, courts should apply judicial estoppel narrowly and only after a full record-based inquiry into intent and surrounding circumstances, not by an irrebuttable presumption.

Maine, 532 U.S. 742 (2001), instructs a flexible, circumstance-specific inquiry rather than a mechanical rule. A presumption of bad faith from “knowledge and motive” alone risks turning an equitable doctrine into a near-mandatory forfeiture that is poorly tailored to the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure and administration framework (including the estate’s interest in undisclosed claims under 11 U.S.C. § 541 and the debtor’s duties under § 521). A holistic approach better accords with history and tradition in equity, promotes practical workability, and avoids unnecessarily punishing creditors by extinguishing potentially valuable estate assets when bankruptcy remedies (e.g., reopening, amendment, trustee control, sanctions) can address nondisclosure. The Fifth Circuit may still find estoppel appropriate on remand, but it must do so based on the totality of the circumstances consistent with New Hampshire v. Maine.

Maine, which cautions against “inflexible prerequisites” and emphasizes considering all relevant circumstances, including whether any inconsistency was the product of “inadvertence or mistake.” A rule that presumes bad faith from knowledge of a claim and a generalized motive to conceal effectively converts that equitable inquiry into a near-automatic bar in bankruptcy, where a debtor almost always has some theoretical incentive, and risks extinguishing property of the estate defined by 11 U.S.C. § 541 to the detriment of creditors rather than vindicating bankruptcy administration tools. Textually, the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure regime (e.g., 11 U.S.C. § 521) supplies mechanisms to correct omissions and protect the estate, and equitable estoppel should not be applied in a way that disregards those structures without examining the debtor’s actual intent and the posture of the bankruptcy case. Consistent with precedent and methodological consistency, courts may infer intent from circumstantial evidence, but they may not treat knowledge-plus-motive as a conclusive proxy for bad faith in lieu of the holistic inquiry New Hampshire requires.

Maine requires a circumstance-specific inquiry rather than a mechanical rule that treats knowledge of the claim plus a generic “motive” to conceal as dispositive of bad faith. In the bankruptcy context, where debtors have broad disclosure duties under 11 U.S.C. §§ 521 and 541, nondisclosure can and should be addressed through bankruptcy tools (amendment, trustee administration, and oversight mechanisms), but extinguishing the claim via a conclusive presumption risks punishing creditors and the estate more than any debtor misconduct. A rigid presumption also undermines procedural fairness by disregarding relevant evidence of mistake, reliance on counsel, timing and corrective disclosures, and the bankruptcy court’s own handling of the omission. Consistent with New Hampshire, courts must assess intent and equities holistically before invoking estoppel to bar a later civil action.
